newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria ex-pm killed, terrorism crackdown urged.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria ex-pm killed, terrorism crackdown urged.

text.p: Bulgarian President Zhelyu Zhelev urged uncompromising measures to fight terrorism after the murder of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov on Wednesday, but parliament said the act should not lead to a state of emergency.
"Decisive and uncompromising measures in the framework of the law are needed against all acts of terrorism," Zhelev said, describing Lukanov's murder as political.

Lukanov, 58, a millionaire businessman and parliamentarian for the ruling Socialists, was found shot dead at his Sofia home. State radio said he had been probably been killed at around 9.30 a.m. (0730 GMT).

"The tragic case with Andrei Lukanov shows again that the fight against terrorism, organised crime and the mafia requires the united efforts of all institutions and cooperation with all countries," Zhelev said in an address to the nation.
Armed police shut major roads linking the Bulgarian capital with frontier checkpoints, witnesses said.

Bulgarian state news agency BTA said police had arrested an elderly man who looked like a tramp near the scene of the killing. But this was not confirmed by police and it was not clear if it represented a hard lead.
The former communist-ruled country of 8.5 million, which is in the grip of dire economic shortages and a crime wave, faces a presidential election on October 27.
Parliament in a statement appealed to the Bulgarian people to stay calm and Zhelev said the murder should not be allowed to fuel pre-election tension.

The silver-haired Lukanov, a former communist politburo member in the communist era, was widely seen as a powerful man in Bulgaria although he held no official post beyond being a deputy for the ruling Socialist Party.
Neighbours of Lukanov said he had been shot twice in the head while leaving his house, but there was no detailed police report.
State radio said the gun used to kill Lukanov may have been fitted with a silencer since neighbours had not heard any noise.

National Security Service chief Dimitar Vladimirov told journalists that Lukanov had been under his unit's protection earlier this year following a specific threat. The protection ended after an "investigation clarified the case," he said.
"This is a political killing and will undoubtedly throw a shadow over the (presidential) election," Socialist parliamentarian Georgi Parvanov said.
Another former prime minister Filip Dimitrov, a deputy for the biggest anti-communist opposition Union of Democratic Forces, described the killing as "a blow to democracy".
Lukanov served as communist prime minister for six months in 1990 but resigned due to widespread public dissatisfaction with the sluggish pace of reform.
Under his rule, Bulgaria declared a moratorium on $12 billion of foreign debt.

In 1992 the public prosecutor launched an inquiry into whether Lukanov misappropriated funds in the 1980s when he was deputy prime minister. He was stripped of parliamentary rights and detained for six months until the case was dropped.
Earlier this year Lukanov criticised the Socialist Party for reviving the functions of the Stalinist state and restoring ties with the secret services.
